hints: Think about what goes into the bridge in Fig. 5.1 and what comes out across the resistor - how does the type of current change?
walkthrough:
**What the circuit does**
Think of $V_{IN}$ as a sine wave that keeps reversing direction. A useful d.c. supply must push charge one way only. Rectification is simply the name for that process of turning a reversing a.c. into a one-direction d.c.
Final answer: Rectification is the conversion of alternating current (a.c.) to direct current (d.c.).

hints: Count the diodes in Fig. 5.1 and recall what happens on both the positive and negative half-cycles of the input.
walkthrough:
**Half-wave versus full-wave**
With one or two diodes you can block one half of the input, giving half-wave. Here you have four diodes in a bridge. That steers current through the load in the same direction on both halves of the input, so both halves are used. That is full-wave rectification.
Final answer: Full-wave rectification.

hints: Follow conventional current through the forward-biased diodes on one half-cycle and see which way it flows through the 1.2 kΩ resistor, from P to Q or Q to P.
walkthrough:
**Trace the diode bridge**
A diode conducts only in the direction of its arrow (triangle to bar). On either half-cycle, one pair of opposite diodes is forward biased and the other pair is reverse biased. Whichever way X-Y polarity is, the bridge always routes current to enter the load at the same terminal.

**Fix the polarity**
Tracing either half-cycle in Fig. 5.1 shows current flows upward through the resistor from Q toward P. So Q stays at higher potential. Label Q + and P -.
Final answer: P is negative (-) and Q is positive (+), so conventional current flows from Q to P outside the resistor, i.e. downwards through $V_{OUT}$ is from Q (+) to P (-).

hints: Compare $V_{IN} = 6.0 \sin 25\pi t$ with the standard $V = V_0 \sin \omega t$ to pick out the peak value and the angular frequency.
Use $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi / T$ to find the input period, then think about why the rectified output repeats twice as often.
Decide what peak height and what time spacing the humps in Fig. 5.2 must have, then choose sensible numbers for the marked grid lines.
walkthrough:
**Read the peak from the equation**
$$V_{IN} = 6.0 \sin 25\pi t$$ is of the form $$V = V_0 \sin \omega t$$ so $V_0 = 6.0\text{ V}$ and $\omega = 25\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}$. Ideal diodes drop no voltage, so the rectified peak is also $6.0\text{ V}$. That sets the height of every hump in Fig. 5.2.

**Find the input period**
Angular frequency links to period by: $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ $$T_{IN} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{25\pi} = 0.080\text{ s}$$ That is the time for one full sine wave at the input.

**Halve the period for full-wave**
Full-wave turns the negative half-cycle positive, so you get two identical humps per input cycle. The output period is half the input period: $$T_{OUT} = \frac{0.080}{2} = 0.040\text{ s}$$ So zeros occur every $0.040\text{ s}$ and peaks are midway between zeros. Labelling the $t$-axis in steps of $0.020\text{ s}$ and the $V_{OUT}$-axis so the peak sits at $6.0\text{ V}$ completes Fig. 5.2.

Final answer: Peak $V_{OUT} = 6.0\text{ V}$. Input period $T_{IN} = 2\pi/25\pi = 0.080\text{ s}$, so rectified period $T_{OUT} = 0.040\text{ s}$. Label $V_{OUT}$ axis e.g. 4 V and 8 V on successive 2 cm marks (peak at 6.0 V) and $t$ axis 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12 s on successive 2 cm marks.

hints: Think where charge must be stored to keep current flowing through the load when the rectified voltage falls to zero - across which component should the capacitor sit?
walkthrough:
**Where smoothing happens**
Smoothing uses a large capacitor that charges to the peak and then discharges through the load when the supply dips. To do that it must see the same voltage as the load, so connect it across P and Q, in parallel with the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor.
Final answer: Connect a capacitor in parallel with the 1.2 kΩ load resistor, i.e. directly between P and Q.

hints: Recall that the capacitor holds the voltage near the peak and only falls slowly while the rectified signal is below it.
Use the 10% ripple stated in (c) to judge how far the voltage should fall between peaks before it rises sharply to the next peak.
walkthrough:
**Shape of smoothed output**
The capacitor charges quickly to the $6.0\text{ V}$ peak, then when the rectified wave falls, the capacitor discharges slowly through the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor. So between peaks draw a gently falling line with negative decreasing gradient, not down to zero.

**Size of the dip**
Maximum to minimum difference is 10% of peak: $$0.10 \times 6.0 = 0.60\text{ V}$$ So each dip goes from $6.0\text{ V}$ down to about $5.4\text{ V}$, then jumps steeply back up to the next $6.0\text{ V}$ peak.

Final answer: Draw a small ripple on Fig. 5.2: voltage falls slowly with decreasing gradient from each 6.0 V peak to 5.4 V, then rises sharply to the next peak. Ripple $= 0.10 \times 6.0 = 0.60\text{ V}$.

hints: Work out the lowest voltage of the ripple from 10% of the 6.0 V peak.
Recall the equation for exponential discharge of a capacitor through a resistor and identify $V_0$, $V$, $R$ and $t$.
Rearrange $V = V_0 \exp(-t/RC)$ to solve for $C$, using discharge time about 0.034 s (approximately the 0.040 s ripple period minus charging time) and $R = 1.2\text{ k}\Omega$.
walkthrough:
**Find the discharge limits**
Peak $V_0 = 6.0\text{ V}$. Ripple is 10%, so drop $= 0.60\text{ V}$. Lowest voltage: $$V = 6.0 - 0.60 = 5.4\text{ V}$$ The capacitor discharges from $6.0\text{ V}$ to $5.4\text{ V}$ through $R = 1.2\times 10^3\ \Omega$ in time $t \approx 0.034\text{ s}$ per ripple cycle.

**Apply exponential discharge**
Discharge follows: $$V = V_0 \exp\left(\frac{-t}{RC}\right)$$ Substitute: $$5.4 = 6.0 \exp\left[\frac{-0.034}{(1.2\times 10^3) C}\right]$$

**Solve for C**
$$\frac{5.4}{6.0} = 0.90 = \exp\left[\frac{-0.034}{(1.2\times 10^3) C}\right]$$ Taking natural logs, $\ln 0.90 = -0.1053$, gives: $$C = \frac{0.034}{(1.2\times 10^3)\times 0.1053} \approx 2.7\times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$$ This large value gives a long time constant $RC$ for good smoothing.
Final answer: Minimum $V = 5.4\text{ V}$, $R = 1.2 \times 10^3\ \Omega$, $t \approx 0.034\text{ s}$. Using $V = V_0 \exp(-t/RC)$ gives $C \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$.
